slides.text:
What Is Logistic Regression?
• A supervised machine-learning algorithm mainly used for classification.
• It estimates the probability that an observation belongs to a class.
• Examples: Pass/Fail, Spam/Not Spam, Fraud/Not Fraud.
For example, suppose a student studies for 6 hours.
Probability of passing = 85%
Probability of failing = 15%
Since the probability of passing is high, the model may predict Pass.
Usually, for binary classification, we use a threshold of 0.5 (50%).
Probability ≥ 0.5 → Pass
Probability < 0.5 → Fail
• Despite the word “regression,” it is commonly used for classification.
• Example: predict whether a student will pass based on study hours.

The Core Idea
• The model calculates a score (Z) from the input features.
• The sigmoid function converts this score into a probability.
• A threshold—often 0.5—turns the probability into a class label.
• If p ≥ 0.5, predict Class 1; otherwise predict Class 0.
Score → Sigmoid → Probability → Class

The Sigmoid Function
• It maps any real-valued score to a value between 0 and 1.
• A value near 0 means low probability of Class 1; near 1 means high probability.
• When z = 0, the sigmoid output is 0.5.
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

Logistic Regression Model
• For one feature: z = b₀ + b₁x.
• For multiple features: z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₙxₙ.
• b₀ is the intercept; b₁, b₂, … are learned coefficients.
• The predicted probability is p = σ(z).
p = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

How the Model Learns
• Start with training examples and known class labels.
• Calculate predicted probabilities using the model.
• Compare predictions with actual labels using a loss function.
A loss function measures how incorrect the predictions are. Logistic Regression commonly 
uses log loss (binary cross-entropy). A lower loss generally indicates better predictions on 
the training examples.
• Adjust coefficients to reduce the loss, commonly using gradient-based optimization.
• Repeat until a stopping condition is reached.

• For one student, suppose the model calculates z = 1.2.

slides.text:
Decision Threshold
• The default threshold is often 0.5, but it is not mandatory.
• A lower threshold predicts more positives and may increase recall and false positives.
Suppose we reduce the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3.
Now, even a probability of 0.40 will be classified as positive.
For example, in disease detection, a lower threshold may help identify more people who 
actually have the disease.
● Advantage: We may detect more actual positive cases (higher recall).
● Disadvantage: We may also incorrectly classify more negative cases as positive (more 
false positives).

Decision Threshold
• A higher threshold predicts fewer positives and may miss more actual positives.
Suppose we increase the threshold from 0.5 to 0.8.
Now, a probability of 0.70 will be classified as negative because it is below 0.8.
● Advantage: The model may produce fewer false positives.
● Disadvantage: It may miss more actual positive cases (more false negatives).
In simple words, the model requires stronger evidence before predicting Class 1.
• Choose a threshold based on the cost of different mistakes.
The best threshold depends on which type of mistake is more serious.
For example, consider a medical test:
● False negative: A sick person is classified as healthy. This could be dangerous.
● False positive: A healthy person is classified as sick. This may lead to unnecessary additional 
testing.
In this case, we may choose a lower threshold to reduce missed cases, while considering the 
additional false positives.

slides.text:
Evaluation Metrics
• Confusion matrix: True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP), False 
Negative (FN).
• Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total predictions.
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP): how many predicted positives are correct.
• Recall = TP / (TP + FN): how many actual positives are found.
• F1-score balances precision and recall.
• AUC summarizes ranking performance across thresholds.

Applications
• Healthcare: estimate a risk category from patient information.
• Banking: classify transactions as potentially fraudulent or not.
• Email: classify messages as spam or not spam.
• Education: predict pass/fail or identify students needing support.
• Marketing: estimate whether a customer may respond to a campaign.

Advantages
• Simple to understand and implement.
• Produces interpretable probabilities.
• Useful as a baseline for many classification tasks.
• Training is often efficient on moderate-sized datasets.
• Coefficients can help explain relationships between features and outcomes.

slides.text:
Limitations
• Assumes a linear relationship between features and log-odds.
• May not capture complex non-linear patterns without feature engineering.
• Can be affected by outliers, multicollinearity, and poor data quality.
• Class imbalance may require suitable metrics or class weighting.
• Predicted probabilities may need calibration.

Key Takeaways
• Logistic regression is primarily a classification method.
• It uses a linear score and sigmoid function to estimate probability.
• A threshold converts probability into a predicted class.
• Evaluate using metrics appropriate to the problem—not accuracy alone.
• Test the model on data not used for training.
